explanation: Claude Code supports nested CLAUDE.md files, so each subproject can carry its own focused, locally-relevant context while the root file covers repo-wide conventions — this scopes context appropriately and helps Claude Code navigate large monorepos efficiently (C). Deleting subprojects (B) isn't a realistic fix for an active monorepo. Manually pasting directory listings every session (D) is repetitive manual work the tool is meant to avoid. One giant root file covering every subproject's internals (A) becomes unwieldy and buries the specific details relevant to whichever subproject is being worked on.

scenario: While fixing a bug, a developer's Claude Code session also needs to research an unrelated part of the codebase to understand a data format, generating a lot of exploratory back-and-forth that isn't relevant to the actual fix.
question: How can subagents help in this situation?
options: Subagents share the exact same context window as the main session, so delegating work to one doesn't change what accumulates in context
Subagents replace the main session entirely so all future work happens only in subagents
The exploratory research can be delegated to a subagent, which does the investigation in its own context and returns a summary, keeping the main session focused on the actual bug fix
Subagents are only useful for writing code, never for research or investigation tasks
explanation: Subagents run in their own separate context and can be delegated a self-contained task like exploratory research, reporting back a concise result instead of flooding the main session's context with intermediate exploration (C). Subagents complement, not replace, the main session (B). They can be used for research and investigation as well as coding tasks (D). Their key value is precisely that they do NOT share the main session's context window (A) — that's why delegating to one keeps the main session cleaner.

scenario: A new engineer joins a team that has been using Claude Code for months. They open the project and ask a teammate how Claude Code already seems to 'know' the team's branching strategy, commit message format, and which directories are auto-generated and should never be edited.
question: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Claude Code automatically infers all team conventions purely by scanning git history with no configuration needed
A teammate must retype these conventions into the chat at the start of every single session
The project's CLAUDE.md file documents these conventions, so that context loads automatically for anyone working in the project with Claude Code
Claude Code has permanent memory of every project it has ever been used on across all users
explanation: This is the core purpose of CLAUDE.md: capturing project conventions once so they're automatically available to anyone using Claude Code on that project (C). Claude Code doesn't retain persistent cross-user memory of every project (D). While it can infer some things from code, reliably knowing conventions like commit format and off-limits directories generally comes from explicit documentation, not just git-history scanning (A). If someone had to retype it every session (B), a new engineer wouldn't observe this behavior working automatically.

scenario: A security-conscious team is configuring Claude Code's permissions for a repository that contains both application code and a `deploy/` directory with scripts that push directly to production.
question: Which permission configuration best balances productivity and safety?
options: Allow routine development commands (tests, linters, builds) broadly, while requiring explicit approval or denying execution of scripts within deploy/
Allow all file edits and shell commands anywhere in the repo, including inside deploy/, to avoid interrupting the developer's flow
Deny all Bash execution repo-wide, including running the test suite, to be maximally cautious
Block Claude Code from reading any file in the repo so it can't accidentally learn about the deploy scripts
explanation: Scoping permissions so routine, low-risk actions are pre-approved while high-risk actions (deploy scripts) require explicit approval or are denied gives the best balance of productivity and safety (A). Allowing everything including deploy scripts (B) creates exactly the production risk the team is worried about. Blocking all file reads (D) would cripple Claude Code's ability to help with the application code too. Denying all Bash execution (C) is overly restrictive and blocks harmless, useful actions like running tests.

scenario: A team notices that whenever Claude Code edits a database migration file, developers occasionally forget to also update the corresponding schema documentation file, causing them to drift out of sync.
question: Which approach would most reliably prevent this drift going forward?
options: Periodically auditing the two files by hand once a quarter
A CLAUDE.md instruction asking Claude Code to 'try to remember' to update docs, with no automated enforcement
A PostToolUse hook that detects edits to migration files and automatically reminds or triggers a check that the schema docs were also updated
A note in the team's onboarding wiki asking developers to remember to update docs
explanation: A hook tied to the relevant tool-use event (editing a migration file) can automatically enforce or flag the related action every time, which is far more reliable than relying on memory (C). An onboarding wiki note (D) is easy to forget in practice, which is the exact problem described. A soft CLAUDE.md request without enforcement (B) is better than nothing but not deterministic. A quarterly manual audit (A) lets drift accumulate for months between checks instead of catching it immediately.

scenario: A developer wants to run Claude Code as part of a nightly automated job that scans the codebase for outdated dependency usage and opens a summary report, with no one watching the terminal.
question: Which combination of features is most appropriate for this job?
options: A hook that fires only when a developer manually opens Claude Code the next morning
Interactive mode plus a custom slash command, run manually each night by whichever developer is on call
Headless/non-interactive execution triggered by the job scheduler, with permissions pre-scoped to the read/write actions the scan needs
MCP integration alone, without addressing how the session itself gets started or how commands get approved
explanation: Unattended, scheduled automation is exactly what headless mode plus pre-scoped permissions supports — the job can start, run, and finish without any human present to respond to prompts (C). Interactive mode run manually (B) requires a human present, defeating the 'nightly, unwatched' requirement. A hook tied to a developer manually opening the tool (A) doesn't run on a schedule independent of human action. MCP integration (D) may help the scan reach external data, but it doesn't address how the session is launched or how it runs unattended, which is the core requirement here.

scenario: A developer sets up an MCP server that gives Claude Code access to their company's internal analytics database, including write access to run arbitrary queries. They plan to use the default configuration for a shared project.
question: What is the most important consideration before enabling this broadly for the team?
options: Whether the scope of access (e.g. read-only vs. write, which tables/actions are exposed) and the permission settings around invoking those MCP tools are appropriately restricted for a shared team context
MCP servers only ever provide read-only access by design, so no additional consideration is needed
Whether the MCP server's name is descriptive enough for developers to recognize it
Whether the analytics database has a visually appealing dashboard UI
explanation: MCP servers can expose powerful actions, including writes, so before rolling one out broadly the team should evaluate and scope exactly what access it grants and how permissions gate its use — the same care applied to any tool with real side effects (A). MCP servers are not inherently read-only (B); this one explicitly has write access to run arbitrary queries. Naming clarity (C) and UI aesthetics (D) are irrelevant to the actual risk of unscoped write access to a production analytics database.

scenario: A team maintains three different custom slash commands for generating release notes, running the full regression suite, and scaffolding a new API endpoint. A new hire asks why these exist instead of just typing out full prompts each time.
question: What is the best explanation of the benefit custom slash commands provide here?
options: They only work for a single specific developer's account and can't be shared with teammates
They replace the need for a CLAUDE.md file in the project
They let the team invoke well-defined, reusable, multi-step prompts consistently and quickly, instead of everyone retyping and possibly varying the same instructions each time
They are required before Claude Code can access any tools at all
explanation: Custom slash commands package a prompt/workflow so it can be invoked consistently and quickly by name, avoiding retyping and reducing variance between team members' phrasing (C). They aren't a prerequisite for tool access in general (D) — that's governed by permissions/settings. They serve a different purpose than CLAUDE.md and don't replace it (B); CLAUDE.md provides persistent background context, while slash commands trigger specific on-demand actions. Project-level slash commands can be checked into the repo and shared across the team, not limited to one developer (A).

scenario: One developer on a shared repository personally likes to auto-approve a specific rarely-used CLI tool for quick experiments, but the rest of the team has agreed that no one should auto-approve that tool because of past mistakes with it.
question: What is the best way to satisfy both the individual preference and the team agreement?
options: Have the developer manually approve the tool every single time and stop wanting the shortcut
Edit the project's shared settings file (checked into the repo) to auto-approve the tool for everyone, since that is the only place permissions can be set

Put the auto-approval in that developer's personal/local settings, which apply only to their own environment, while the shared project settings committed to the repo remain unchanged for the rest of the team
Ask the whole team to change their agreement so it matches what one developer wants
explanation: Claude Code separates shared, repo-level settings from personal/local settings, so an individual can adjust their own environment's permissions without changing what's committed and applied to the rest of the team (C). Editing the shared project settings (B) would impose the individual's preference on everyone, violating the team agreement. Changing the team's agreement (D) isn't a settings solution and overrides a decision made for good reason. Forcing manual approval every time (A) ignores that personal-scope settings exist to solve exactly this kind of individual customization.
